lesson.title: Turning "Approximately Normal" Into an Actual Number
lesson.summary: Once the CLT conditions are satisfied, the normal distribution can be used to calculate real probabilities about a sample statistic, using the same z-score method learned for individual normal variables.
lesson.body:
Knowing that a sampling distribution is approximately normal is only useful if you can turn that fact into actual numbers. The normal approximation is the technique of doing exactly that: once the CLT conditions from the last section are met, you can treat the sampling distribution of p-hat or x-bar as a normal curve with a specific mean and standard deviation, and then use the same z-score machinery used for any normal random variable to compute probabilities.

For a sample proportion, the sampling distribution is centered at the true population proportion p, with standard deviation equal to the square root of p times (1 minus p) divided by n. For a sample mean, it is centered at the true population mean mu, with standard deviation equal to sigma divided by the square root of n, when the population standard deviation sigma is known. Either way, once you have a mean and a standard deviation for the sampling distribution, a value of the statistic converts into a z-score exactly the way any normal value does: z equals the value minus the mean, divided by the standard deviation. That z-score can then be looked up in a standard normal table, or evaluated with normal probability software, to get an actual probability.

This matters because it is the bridge between abstract theory and answerable questions. Without the normal approximation, "the sampling distribution is approximately normal" is just a shape description. With it, you can answer concrete questions like how unusual it would be to see a sample proportion this high if the true proportion really is 20%. That kind of question is the seed of statistical inference, which starts in the next chapter.

A company claims that 20% of its customers use its mobile app, so p equals 0.20. A random sample of 200 customers is surveyed. First check conditions: n times p equals 200 times 0.20, which is 40, and n times (1 minus p) equals 200 times 0.80, which is 160. Both are at least 10, so the normal approximation is appropriate. The sampling distribution of p-hat is centered at 0.20 with standard deviation equal to the square root of (0.20 times 0.80) divided by 200, which is the square root of 0.0008, or about 0.0283. Suppose the survey actually finds p-hat equals 0.25. Its z-score is (0.25 minus 0.20) divided by 0.0283, which is about 1.77. Looking up z equals 1.77 in a standard normal table gives a cumulative probability of about 0.9616, meaning the probability of seeing a z-score above 1.77 is about 1 minus 0.9616, or 0.0384. In other words, if the company's 20% claim is true, only about a 3.8% chance exists that a random sample of 200 customers would show a sample proportion of 25% or higher just from ordinary sampling variability. That small probability is a signal worth paying attention to, and reasoning like this, using a sample result to question a claim about a population, is precisely what the next chapter formalizes as statistical inference.
